evidence_quotes.quote: The article examines current global trends in the expansion of water and sanitation services, and discusses the systemic conditions affecting their provision.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 8 of 16 (The Systemic Conditions: Mainstream WSS Public Policy, p. 111)
evidence_quotes.quote: In particular, we focus here on two aspects that are core elements of mainstream WSS policy: (a) the reversal of the values of universalism in the access to essential public services, and (b) the attempt to transform the provision of essential public services into a commercial enterprise, and preferably into one that is privately run and profit oriented.

For this reason, the implementation of public policy and management models in WSS must consider the existence of systemic conditions; that is, factors and processes that are mostly external to the specific field and internal logic of essential public services but that often determine the conditions under which these services are organised and delivered.

It is our hypothesis that achieving success in the design and implementation of present and future WSS policies as those required to meet the MDGs can only happen through the amalgamation of a similarly broad and universalistic alliance of social forces that may help to foster a new vision for defending the common good.

As shown in Table 1, predictions based on the interpolation of current trends suggest that not only the MDGs for WSS may not be reached, but actually regions such as sub-Saharan Africa will experience a significant increase in the absolute number of unserved people.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines universalisation of and household/population access to drinking water and sanitation services (WSS), including global MDG coverage trends and water affordability/poverty.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: YES — discusses institutional, governance, and policy factors in water and sanitation (neoliberal water policy reforms, commercialisation, commodification, privatisation vs public provision, and absence of regulatory frameworks). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: NO — explicitly frames its subject as macro-level 'systemic conditions' external to the specific running of WSS and critiques global neoliberal ideology and commodification in general narrative terms rather than empirically examining a specific operational rule-type mechanism governing household access (though even if general mentions of utility privatisation and ability-to-pay principles were credited, the paper still fails c3_empirical).
criterion_notes.c3: Explicitly published as an 'Overview Article' (narrative sociological exploration and critical policy essay introducing themes in a special issue). Contains no primary empirical data collection, no qualitative or quantitative research methodology, and no systematic empirical synthesis method; relies solely on narrative literature commentary and two descriptive summary tables adapted from WHO-UNICEF (2006). Excluded under E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Does not report empirical study outcomes from an original investigation or systematic synthesis; only reproduces illustrative secondary aggregate coverage figures from WHO-UNICEF (2006) (Tables 1 and 2) and cites secondary estimates of water debt/water poverty in England and Wales within a narrative essay.
criterion_notes.c5: Lacks an identifiable empirical study design, analytical sample, and operationalised exposure-outcome analysis because it is a conceptual and policy overview essay.

study_design: Narrative sociological overview / policy commentary essay (non-empirical Overview Article)
country: Global (illustrative secondary examples from sub-Saharan Africa, Europe, England and Wales, Brazil, China, India, Mexico, Bolivia, Israel, USA, and Argentina)
exposure: Macro-level systemic conditions (structural social inequalities) and mainstream neoliberal water and sanitation policies (commercialisation, commodification, privatisation)
rationale: This paper (labeled 'Overview Article' in Journal of Comparative Social Welfare) is a non-empirical sociological essay and critical policy overview examining global trends in water and sanitation universalisation, structural social inequalities, and neoliberal water reforms since the 1980s. Although it addresses water and sanitation access (c1) and discusses governance/policy themes that satisfy the plain wording of Criterion 2 (and treats macro-level systemic conditions and ideological commodification as policy background rather than analysing a concrete rule-type access mechanism under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading), it reports no primary empirical research, no qualitative or quantitative data collection/analysis methods, and no systematic synthesis methodology, citing only secondary WHO-UNICEF summary tables and existing literature. Under both the narrow and plain readings of Criterion 2, it must be excluded as E05 (No empirical evidence).
